newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Prudent budget to spark rally.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Prudent budget to spark rally.

text.p: UK gilts may outperform their European counterparts this week and stage a minor rally at the short end -- provided Chancellor Kenneth Clarke delivers a prudent budget as expected on Tuesday.
But analysts say any great sigh of relief will be short-lived as inflation and interest rate concerns return to dog the market.
Domestic investors, reluctant to take positions ahead of the budget, should pile back into UK debt provided Clarke resists the temptation for large, vote-grabbing tax cuts.

"Clarke's aim in this budget...is to win the election, but in a way that doesn't damage the prospects for the public finances, and to deflect pressure for another interest rate rise," said Union Discount chief economist Philip Shaw.
"If he manages to accomplish this, we may well see short dated gilts rally because of some change in interest rate expectations."

Robust economic growth, strong money supply data and signs of a resurgence in UK inflation have prompted investors to revise up their expectations for interest rates in recent months, leading to curve flattening.
"The budget should prompt some reversal of the recent flattening," Shaw said.
Analysts said gilts were in for a roller-coaster ride as the nation's accounts come under scrutiny on Tuesday.

Clarke is expected to deliver an eye-catching one penny cut in the basic rate of income tax, but that aside, only to tinker with the tax system, allowing room to increase spending on the politically sensitive areas of health and education.
Analysts said a prudent budget should allow gilts to gain ground on European debt.

"On the back of the budget from Clarke we believe that gilts will be able to outperform Bunds with the 10-year spread tightening in, possibly by as much as 10 basis points," said Tom Rayner at Societe Generale.
By 1256 GMT on Monday the gilt/Bund spread was at 177 bps.
UBS gilts analyst Andrew Roberts said there was scope for the Bund spread to dip below 170 basis points.
"If the budget doesn't shock there will be some money coming in," he said.

"But I don't see too much downside to the spread because there'll be an incentive to take profits after the budget, especially with a gilt auction the week after and the monetary meeting where you've got a potential rate hike."

Clarke is due to hold his next monetary policy meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on December 11. With consumer spending on the rise and signs of inflation re-emerging, Clarke is under pressure to raise rates again ahead of the election which must be held by May 22 next year.
Roberts said the upside for short sterling in the post-budget scramble to take positions would be limited.
"I can't see it helping short sterling immensely because it's quite rational. I think it's got more to go down yet," he said, adding the market may have factored in the budget news.
"There is a risk of buying on the rumour and selling on the fact of the budget," he said.
A limited crop of UK data this week starts with trade on Wednesday and final October M4 money supply data on Friday.

The Reuters consensus forecast is for the UK's global trade deficit to widen to one billion stg in September from 584 million in August. The non-EU trade deficit is seen at 835 million stg in October from 851 million in September.
